generated_by: prism-parity:tools/generate-session-keys.php for php; the ports' own runners for ts and py. Every key is execution output.
pins_note: A session key is an ADDRESS. It is what lets a PHP application and a TypeScript or Python agent resolve the same conversation, and it is the string a store is keyed by. If it drifts, nothing errors: each language happily reads and writes its own key, and the two simply stop seeing each other's turns. There is no failure mode louder than a conversation that appears empty.

cases.title: the ordinary session
cases.notes: The control. A Laravel morph class, a numeric id, the default scope — what the overwhelming majority of real sessions look like.

cases.title: a non-default scope
cases.notes: Scope is the last segment and is not hashed. Pins that two scopes for one participant are different addresses — which is the whole point of scope.

cases.title: a different participant id
cases.notes: The id is not hashed either. If it were, this suite could not tell an id collision from a type collision.

cases.title: a different participant type
cases.notes: Same id, different type. User 7 and Team 7 must not share a conversation, and the hashed type segment is the only thing keeping them apart.

cases.title: a short morph alias rather than a class name
cases.notes: Laravel's `enforceMorphMap` makes this the common production shape, not an edge case. It also proves the hash is over the type STRING as given — a language that normalised or namespaced it would diverge here and nowhere else.

cases.title: a zero id
cases.notes: Falsy in every language involved. A truthiness check anywhere on the id path turns this into a different address, or an empty segment.

cases.title: a ULID primary key
cases.notes: Not every application has integer keys. Pins that a long non-numeric id is carried through whole rather than cast.

cases.title: a non-ASCII type name
cases.notes: sha1 is over BYTES, so this row pins that all three languages hash the same UTF-8 encoding of the same string. A language hashing UTF-16 code units, or one that latin-1'd it first, produces a different digest from identical-looking source.

cases.title: a scope containing the segment separator
cases.notes: Colons are the separator and nothing escapes them. Recorded because it is the shape that makes the key AMBIGUOUS to parse — not a bug today, since nothing parses a key back into parts, but the row that would go red the moment something tried.

divergence_note: Every row agrees, on the first run, with no fix needed -- the only satellite suite so far where that was true. Worth stating because it is the most consequential address in the ecosystem: if a session key drifted, nothing would error. Each language would read and write its own key perfectly happily, and a PHP application and a TypeScript agent would simply stop seeing each other's turns. A conversation that appears empty has no louder failure mode behind it.
